summary: This revision extends a simulation study of finite-sample negative bias in the plug-in semantic-entropy (SE) estimator used for LLM uncertainty quantification. The original contribution (unchanged from v1, and independently re-verified in this pass) is a Dirichlet-categorical simulation across 15 (K x concentration) cells showing plug-in SE is negatively biased by 28-84% of its bias-corrected value, that a Miller-Madow correction removes most of this bias while leaving AUROC ranking performance essentially untouched at K<=5, and that entropy beats a top-1 self-consistency baseline once K>=5. This revision directly answers three round-1 reviewer questions with two new experiments: (1) the bias/rank-invariance pattern is reproduced under non-Dirichlet (bimodal, power-law) cluster-mass shapes, ruling out a Dirichlet-specific artifact, and (2) a label-flip clustering-noise model shows entailment-clustering error partially cancels the sampling bias and, at K=10/epsilon=0.2, causes the MM correction to overshoot into a small positive bias (+0.033) -- a genuinely new and non-obvious finding about when the correction should not be applied naively. I re-ran experiment_v2.py end-to-end and every headline number quoted in the new Results subsections (bimodal and power-law bias/AUROC/p-values at K=3,5,10,20, and the epsilon-sweep bias values at K=5,10 including the +0.033 overshoot) reproduced to the reported precision.
strengths:
- Full reproducibility of the new material: independently re-running experiment_v2.py reproduced every quoted number in the new subsections essentially exactly, e.g. bimodal K=3 bias -0.433->-0.311 (28.1% reduction, I got -0.4331/-0.3114/28.09%), power-law K=20 bias -0.140->-0.046 (67.2%, I got -0.1397/-0.0459/67.16%), and critically the eps=0.2, K=10 MM-overshoot to +0.033 (I got +0.0325) -- this is the paper's most surprising claim and it holds up under independent execution
- The two new experiments are a genuine, substantive response to the round-1 questions rather than token additions: the clustering-noise result (label noise partially cancels sampling bias and can flip the sign of the correction's residual error) is a real, non-obvious finding with practical implications (don't apply MM correction blind to entailment-model error rate), not just a robustness checkbox
- The paper is transparent about what remains unaddressed: Limitations correctly notes the shape sweep is still parametric/not fit to real per-query cluster data, and the label-flip model is i.i.d. and doesn't capture structured entailment failure modes -- appropriately scoped claims rather than overclaiming the new experiments as a full resolution
- The core original contribution (rank-vs-absolute-value dissociation, mechanistically explained by the MM term depending only on C_obs) remains sound and was already verified in round 1; this revision does not alter or weaken it
weaknesses:
- The paper's own Artifacts list ("experiment.py, experiment_v2.py, run_log.txt, run_log_v2.txt, results.json, results_v2.json, all in this directory") is not accurate: run_log_v2.txt does not exist in the directory I reviewed (verified via `ls`), so one of six claimed artifacts is missing
- The claimed combined runtime of "28.4s + 27.0s on CPU" for experiment.py + experiment_v2.py understates the actual cost substantially: my independent run of experiment_v2.py alone took 145.3s (script-reported elapsed_seconds) / 146.6s wall-clock, roughly 5.4x the paper's stated 27.0s figure. This could reflect a slower CPU in my environment, but the paper presents the runtime as a specific, reproducible fact ("Combined runtime: 28.4s + 27.0s on CPU") without qualification, and I have no way to confirm the original hardware -- it's a discrepancy between the stated number and what the exact same code produces when actually run
- Still entirely simulation-based with no real LLM or entailment-model data (a pre-existing, disclosed limitation, not new to this revision), so the central bias-magnitude numbers remain unvalidated against a real SE pipeline; the new clustering-noise model is an i.i.d. label-flip toy, not fit to any measured entailment-model error rate, so its quantitative overshoot threshold (epsilon=0.2, K=10) should not be read as a validated real-world trigger point, only as a qualitative existence proof that overshoot is possible
questions:
1. Can you regenerate run_log_v2.txt (or remove it from the Artifacts list if it was never meant to be included) so the artifact listing matches what's actually in the directory?
2. Is the 27.0s runtime figure specific to a particular machine/environment? Given the run I performed took ~5x longer, it would help to state the hardware (or note runtime is environment-dependent) rather than presenting it as a fixed fact.
3. For the clustering-noise overshoot result, do you have any sense of what real entailment-model error rates (e.g., off-the-shelf NLI models used for SE clustering) look like empirically, to judge whether epsilon=0.2 is a realistic or worst-case value for the overshoot to actually arise in practice?
